title: Elbridge Colby on the Opportunities of the “Donroe Doctrine”
gist: Elbridge Colby, U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy, uses a Cusco defense-ministers speech to formalize the "Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine" (the "Donroe Doctrine"): Washington will use military force against narco-terrorist networks in Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America, deny any outside actor access to key hemispheric terrain, and press Latin American states to raise defense spending well above the sub-1%-of-GDP levels some now run.

insights.claim: The U.S. Department of War has formally named its Western Hemisphere strategy the "Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine" — colloquially the "Donroe Doctrine" — committing the United States to protect access to key terrain throughout Latin America and the Caribbean and to deny adversaries the ability to position forces or threatening capabilities in the hemisphere.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: An explicit sphere-of-influence doctrine raises the policy risk premium on Chinese- or Russian-linked infrastructure, port and telecom assets across LatAm; investors should treat 'key terrain' assets as politically contestable.
insights.quote: protect our Homeland and our access to key terrain throughout the region. We will deny adversaries’ ability to position forces or other threatening capabilities in our Hemisphere.
insights.locator: We call this strategy the Trump Corollary

insights.claim: The doctrine is codified in official strategy documents, being guided by what the Department of War calls a "flexible realism" articulated in the 2025 National Security Strategy and the 2026 National Defense Strategy.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: The hemispheric turn is institutionalized in doctrine, not a one-off campaign — it survives news cycles and should be modeled as a multi-year procurement and deployment trend.
insights.quote: guided by a flexible realism articulated in the 2025 National Security Strategy and 2026 National Defense Strategy
insights.locator: President Donald Trump and the Department of War

insights.claim: Colby pre-empts the imperialism critique by arguing the Monroe Doctrine is "often misunderstood" and that the version being revived is about empowering the independence, security and prosperity of Latin American and Caribbean nations rather than subordinating them.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: The framing is the sales pitch to regional governments; watch whether partner capitals accept it, since regional buy-in determines whether U.S. operations are 'partner-led' or unilateral.
insights.quote: This properly understood Monroe Doctrine is not the distorted version; rather, it is precisely about empowering, enabling, and supporting the independence, security, and prosperity of the Latin American and Caribbean nations.
insights.locator: Of course, we recognize that the Monroe Doctrine is controversial

insights.claim: Operation Southern Spear is cited as the operational proof of the new posture — the Department of War going "on offense" against narco-terrorist networks rather than merely supporting law-enforcement efforts.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: A named, ongoing military operation signals sustained deployment costs and escalation risk in the Caribbean basin — relevant to shipping insurance, Venezuelan risk pricing and defense contractors.
insights.quote: This has been amply demonstrated in Operation Southern Spear, in which the Department has gone on offense against narco-terrorist networks
insights.locator: Instead, we will bring all the assets

insights.claim: The U.S. explicitly equates Latin American drug cartels with jihadist terrorist organizations, signaling that counterterrorism rules of engagement rather than counter-narcotics policing will govern American action.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: The ISIS analogy is the legal and rhetorical scaffolding for lethal strikes; expect further kinetic actions and the accompanying diplomatic friction over sovereignty.
insights.quote: We will not treat the ISIS, the al Qaedas of this hemisphere, with kid gloves.
insights.locator: At the same time, it is a signal

insights.claim: The stated end-state is partner-led joint kinetic operations, with U.S. forces acting as force multipliers rather than the primary executors, and Washington supplying capabilities partners must then master themselves.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: Implies a pipeline of foreign military sales, ISR and training contracts to LatAm partners — a durable demand channel for U.S. defense exporters.
insights.quote: We see partner-led, joint kinetic operations with partner nations as force multipliers, as the way to lasting and durable progress against these perils.
insights.locator: Instead, we will bring all the assets

insights.claim: Colby draws a hard conditionality line: U.S. hemispheric support will only work if regional governments demonstrate political will and seriousness, implying support can be withdrawn from partners judged insufficiently committed.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: Conditionality creates a bifurcation trade across LatAm sovereigns — cooperative governments get security and investment tailwinds, resistant ones get pressure.
insights.quote: This will only work if our neighbors demonstrate the political will, clarity, and seriousness needed for success.
insights.locator: But, as we have learned through hard experience

insights.claim: Some Western Hemisphere countries spend less than 1% of GDP on national defense, a level the U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy calls a violation of common sense given the narco-terrorist threats they face.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: Explicit U.S. pressure for higher LatAm defense budgets is a fiscal-expenditure signal — watch Colombia, Peru, Ecuador and Caribbean budgets for defense line-item expansion and the associated deficit impact.
insights.quote: Indeed, some spend less than 1% of GDP on national defense. This violates common sense.
insights.locator: Third, it is critical that our hemispheric neighbors invest more

insights.claim: The NATO-style 3.5% core military plus 1.5% security-related spending benchmark is being explicitly held up to Latin American governments as the standard other U.S. allies are moving toward.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: Importing the European burden-sharing target into the hemisphere sets a public yardstick against which LatAm governments will be judged — and a sizeable potential addressable market for arms suppliers.
insights.quote: our allies around the world, including in Europe, are now moving toward significantly higher spending – 3.5% on core military spending and an additional 1.5% on security-related expenditures
insights.locator: In the meantime, our allies around the world

insights.claim: Unlike U.S. alliance demands in Europe and Asia, hemispheric partners are not being asked to project power outside their own region — the ask is purely denial of key assets to outside actors within the hemisphere.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: A low-cost ask designed to maximize compliance; the practical implication is pressure on port, canal, mining and telecom concessions held by extra-hemispheric actors.
insights.quote: we will not ask neighbors to project power out of this region. All we ask of our neighbors is that they work with us to deny any actor the ability to claim and exploit key assets here in this hemisphere.
insights.locator: As the U.S. works with allies and partners

insights.claim: Protecting critical assets is framed as a precondition for foreign investment and development, tying the security agenda directly to capital formation in partner economies.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: Washington is signaling that security guarantees and investment flows move together — a channel through which U.S. policy could steer FDI toward compliant jurisdictions.
insights.quote: We also call on regional partners to protect their critical assets. This is not only a precondition for investment and development.
insights.locator: We also call on regional partners

insights.claim: The Trump administration's defense policy leadership explicitly declares the post-1995 unipolar framework — liberal internationalism and the "rules-based international order" — dead as an organizing principle for U.S. strategy.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
entities: Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas
insights.so_what: Confirms a durable regime shift in U.S. foreign policy assumptions; models built on multilateral-institution continuity need re-basing toward transactional, regional bargaining.
insights.quote: A realistic outlook based on geography and national interests took a back seat to liberal internationalism and the “rules-based international order.”
insights.locator: Much has changed in the Western Hemisphere

insights.claim: The prior generation's Latin America approach is characterized as benign neglect that turned malign, with the hemisphere treated as "a backwater in America's strategic imagination" that elites viewed as beneath the dignity of the armed forces.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: The neglect narrative justifies a large, sustained reallocation of military attention and budget toward SOUTHCOM's area of responsibility and away from other theaters.
insights.quote: the very hemisphere where our own country is located was – frankly – a backwater in America’s strategic imagination
insights.locator: And this is needed. For the last generation

insights.claim: Colby names Maduro's Venezuela, Ortega's Nicaragua and Morales's Bolivia as "hard-left regimes that enabled narco-terrorists" and causally links them to mass migration and the U.S. border crisis.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: Naming specific regimes as the causal source of U.S. domestic harm is the predicate for coercive action; Venezuela in particular carries elevated regime-change and oil-supply optionality.
insights.quote: Hard-left regimes that enabled narco-terrorists multiplied across our hemisphere from Nicolás Maduro’s Venezuela to Daniel Ortega’s Nicaragua to Evo Morales’s Bolivia.
insights.locator: In recent decades, Latin America’s scourge of narco-terrorism

insights.claim: Hundreds of thousands of Americans and their neighbors have been killed by lethal drugs and narco-terrorist violence in recent years, a figure used to justify treating the hemisphere as a homeland-defense theater.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: The casualty framing converts a law-enforcement issue into a war footing, which lowers the political threshold for military action in the region.
insights.quote: A record number of Americans and their neighbors – hundreds of thousands in recent years – were killed by lethal drugs and narco-terrorist violence.
insights.locator: In recent decades, Latin America’s scourge

insights.claim: A former U.S. secretary of state's declaration just over a decade ago that the Monroe Doctrine was "over" is presented as the origin point of a policy failure that weakened rather than strengthened the hemisphere.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: The administration is deliberately reversing a named prior policy position, which makes partial rollback under a future administration a live but explicitly contested scenario.
insights.quote: Just over a decade ago, a U.S. secretary of state declared proudly that the Monroe Doctrine was “over.”

insights.claim: Colby argues the United States uniquely does not need imperial possessions or dependencies even on strict realpolitik grounds, citing its size, largest and most dynamic market, most productive economy, dominant currency and raw-material stores.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: The self-sufficiency argument is the intellectual basis for a doctrine of denial rather than extraction — meaning U.S. pressure will target adversary access more than local ownership.
insights.quote: The upshot is that we do not need imperial possessions or dependencies, even from a strictly realpolitik point of view. This differentiates the United States from most historical empires.
insights.locator: The fact is that the United States doesn’t need

insights.claim: The doctrine inverts the development-first sequencing of past U.S. Latin America policy, asserting that security is a basic prerequisite for national development rather than a competitor for the same aid dollars.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: Signals aid budgets will be re-weighted toward security assistance and away from 'root causes' development programs — a reallocation visible in State and USAID-successor line items.
insights.quote: Our approach does not juxtapose defense against development, like the visions of the past; rather, it recognizes the verity that security is a basic prerequisite for national development.
insights.locator: Now, this has been said before

insights.claim: The implied U.S. preference is for capable, well-armed Latin American states rather than weak clients — an inversion of the historical U.S. instinct to prefer pliable, dependent neighbors.
insights.speaker: ELBRIDGE COLBY
insights.so_what: If followed through, this means fewer restrictions on capability transfers to LatAm militaries and a rising regional arms-procurement cycle.
insights.quote: We want strong, reliable, and effective partners, not feeble and dependent ones.
insights.locator: Under President Trump’s leadership and with the Trump Corollary

top_entities: Conference of Defense Ministers of the Americas
